The controller is split in two files, on purpose: `main.jl` is the simulation of the day, the receding
horizon loop that measures, calls the optimizer and applies the first control; `MPC_iteration.jl` is the
optimization problem alone, written in JuMP and handed to a solver. That is the separation we keep in every
case study of the course: the loop belongs to the application, the optimization problem belongs to the
controller.

The problem solved at every step is the one of the lecture, with the consumer sign convention, so power
consumed is positive and $u > 0$ charges the storage:

$$
\min \sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big[\alpha\, p_i^2 + \beta\,(x_i - x^{ref})^2\Big] + \beta_f\,(x_{N+1}-x^{ref})^2
$$

subject to the balance at the point of connection $p_i = u_i + p^{pev}_i - p^{res}_i$, the dynamics of the
storage $x_{i+1} = x_i + (T/3600)\,u_i$, the measured state $x_1 = x_k$, and the bounds on $u$, $x$ and $p$.
Both the charging demand $p^{pev}$ and the renewable generation $p^{res}$ are assumed known over the window.

The code uses [HiGHS](https://highs.dev), which is open source and is installed in the
[software setup](../../setup.qmd) of the course. Gurobi is one commented line away, and nothing else changes:
that is the point of a modelling language like JuMP.
